Programming makes for a very interesting and engaging avenue to learning math. For many students learning math, the elements which give it its appeal have been stripped away. A teacher tells you what to do, and hands out assignments, which can seem like doing chores. It could even be like memorizing lyrics in a foreign language by rote, having no understanding of the words, the culture or history of the song, or even knowing that it's a song at all. But for the programmer the tables are turned. You think of what you want the computer to do for you, and you have to figure out how to explain the instructions in its language; and it follows those instructions precisely and without hesitation. With the computer as your genie you become the supreme master. Not only can you play games on your computer, you can have it create entire worlds only to serve as your playground.

But with great power comes great responsibility. Remember the story of the monkey's paw? The owner was granted three wishes. The first was for monetary fortune, and the wish was granted by giving them compensation for a factory accident which killed their son. You have to think very carefully about what you're telling the computer to do. It does whatever you ask without question, it doesn't care about the consequences, and may not warn you if you're making a mistake.

Now Python isn't the computer's native language, machine code is. So if we really want to see how the computer thinks, we should learn a bit about machine code and assembly language. The way we think is fairly different from the way a computer thinks. It's hard to teach a computer English, and it's hard to teach a human machine code. So we have intermediate languages which are easier for both to pick up, such as C++, Python, and Assembly. So we can write our source code in the programming language of our choice, and it gets translated into machine code instructions so we can run it. Assembly is the closest to machine code. In some ways assembly language is one of the simplest and easiest languages to understand; but it's harder for most people to use it, because it makes you handle more details. I'll be talking about Intel x86 Assembly language for Linux. Let's look at our summation loop in Assembly:

mov eax,0
mov ecx,100

sum:
add eax,ecx
dec ecx
jnz sum

In assembly language there are two main places to store our variables. In registers (such as: EAX, EBX, ECX...), or in RAM. Here we're using 32 bit registers. The instructions we can use are mostly simple operations such as add, sub, mul, div. Let's walk through this step by step.

 mov eax,0 ;we need something to store our sum, so we'll start by clearing out eax to get it ready
 mov ecx,100 ;we're going to start with one hundred and count down from there. 

sum:add eax,ecx ; here we simply add whatever's in ecx to the value in eax.
 ;The first time here, that will set eax to 100+0, which is 100
 dec ecx ;decrement ecx by 1 this brings it down to 99 the first time through
 jnz sum ;if ecx is not zero we'll jump back to where the lable sum is located.
 ;ECX is 99, the first time here, so go back to sum and repeat.
 ;by the time ecx reaches zero, we will have added every number from 1 to 100 into eax

Although this code will add all the numbers together, it won't display the result. So how can we get it to do that? Let's look at how to print messages in Assembly.

section .text
 global _start ;must be declared for using gcc
_start: ;tell linker entry point
 mov edx, len ;message length
 mov ecx, msg ;message to write
 mov ebx, 1 ;file descriptor (stdout)
 mov eax, 4 ;system call number (sys_write)
 int 0x80 ;call kernel
 mov eax, 1 ;system call number (sys_exit)
 int 0x80 ;call kernel

section .data

msg db 'Hello, world!',0xa ;our dear string
len equ $ - msg ;length of our dear string

You can head over to https://www.tutorialspoint.com/compile_assembly_online.php to run this program. It's up to the operating system (a special type of program) to print output. So what we do here is fill out the registers with the required information, and hand everything off to the OS with a system call from interupt 0x80. Note, the 0x prefix indicates that this is hexadecimal (base 16, a shorthand for binary), and not regular decimal. So after the Operating System is finished printing the message, it points the CPU back to the next instruction to continue execution. Or, if the exit code is given, it closes our program.

Let's look at our message string: 'Hello, world',0xa It's stored in a segment of RAM at a 32 bit address we labeled msg. Actually to be more precise, the letter 'H' is located at that address, and the other characters are its neighbors. Everything is stored as a binary number, so the letters are actually eight bit ASCII codes. The 0xa, is the new line symbol. So what's that len on the next line? That's a macro. Whenever you write len somewhere else, the assembler will translate it to the length of msg, which it calculated by subtracting the address of msg from the address following the 0xa.

So are we ready to print our output? Not quite yet, we have to translate the result left in eax (a 32 bit integer), to an ASCII string stored in RAM. How do we do that? The div instruction will let us divide eax by ten and save the remainder in dx. We can use that to produce our digits in right to left order. The ASCII codes for the decimal numbers are: '0'=48, '1'=49, '2'=50, and so on. So if we add 48 to the remainder it will display everything properly. So let's put this into action!

There was one time I mentioned to another programmer that I was working on Assembly; and he asked me "What are you doing playing around in Assembly Language?". Assembly is kind of like the Latin of programming. Some people are very impressed by anyone who possesses such arcane knowledge, others see it as an anachronism.

So with all the effort that's been invested in creating new languages so we don't have to bother with the low level details, what's the point of studying Assembly? Well someone has to work with the low level tools or we wouldn't have any high level tools. Sometimes we can squeeze some extra performance out of the computer with some well designed Assembly. But the main reason to study Assembly is to understand the computer better, so hopefully you can apply your higher level programming skills more effectively.

Assembly was a very painful learning experience for me. The way it works is completely antithetical to my intuitive "right brained" thinking style. But now that I better understand how the computer thinks, it's helped me understand my own thought process. When you're programming, you're basically having to scrutinize your own thoughts, examining them until you understand them well enough to reconstruct them on the computer. The fewer details your programming tools handle for you, the more thoroughly you have dissect your ideas. It makes you take less for granted. Programming has changed the way I think about everything. Even when I write in English, the approach I take is based on how I write a computer program. If you want to get better at Chess, or Othello, just think about how you would program the computer to do what you do. You'll see what your doing more clearly. If you want to understand math better, I highly recommend combining your math skills with programming.

Now, since the computer originated as the tool of the mathematician, shouldn't there be some overlap between programming and mathematics? Computers perform arithmetic and logical operations. Programming languages picked up some elements of algebraic notation. Does math have elements of programming in it? You could say Russel and Whitehead's Principia Mathematica and related works are the assembly language of math. George Boole founded the field of information theory. Allen Turing developed the theory of computation. Ray Solomonoff contributed to algorithmic probability. One could explain math simply as the theory of computation and related fields. Mathematicians write programs in their own languages. They are the programmers of the universe (or at least of hypothetical scenarios).
